title: Don't rely on deeds
hookLine: a sign of relying on your deeds is losing hope when you slip (Hikam 1, paraphrased)
tomorrow: why would a seed choose to stay buried in the dark?

lines: ONE BAD GRADE, ALL HOPE GONE.
cards: One bad grade, one rejected pitch, one sharp comment from someone you respect, and suddenly it's all over: every plan, every hope, gone in an afternoon. The spiral is fast and very convincing.
It feels like seeing clearly at last. What does a crash like that actually reveal? Ibn Ata'illah opens the Hikam with exactly this.
Among the signs that you're relying on your deeds, he says, is losing hope when you slip.

teach.b: The crash shows where your weight was. If your hope collapses at one slip, it was resting on your record, and records wobble. He isn't saying deeds don't matter; the whole book assumes you'll keep doing good.
He's asking what you lean on. A hadith in al-Bukhari makes the same turn. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said no one will enter Paradise by their deeds alone.
Not even you? his companions asked.
Not even me, he said, unless God covers me with his mercy. So you keep working, and you lean on mercy.
Now, hold up the week beside that first saying. Stillness making room in prayer: the heart of prayer. A fast that reaches the eyes and tongue: the fast of the heart.
A fogged glass that isn't broken: the mirror. One steady hand, one open: two halves. A last book that sorts the day: preparing to meet him.
A small book read slowly: wisdoms. Every one of those is a practice, and every one could become a new record to lean on. Ibn Ata'illah's first word guards against exactly that.

teach.h: DO THEM ALL, REST ON NONE.

how: Teachers of the Hikam begin with this first aphorism; Muslims keep up prayer and good deeds while hoping in God's mercy rather than in their own record.

games.q: what does “don't rely on deeds” mean?
o: keep doing good, but lean on God, not your record
stop doing good deeds, since only faith matters
never trust anyone else to do your work for you

games.q: the week and the first saying — tap the pairs.
p: a sign of leaning on your record
unless God covers me with mercy
the last book of the Revival

s: Ibn Ata'illah says good deeds don't matter
the book assumes you'll keep doing good. his question is what you lean on.
a hadith in al-Bukhari says no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, not even the Prophet
not even me, he said, unless God covers me with his mercy.
a big crash after one mistake shows you care deeply about God
the Hikam reads it as a sign your hope was resting on your record.

games.q: your friend has prayed on time for a whole month, then misses one and says she's ruined everything and might as well stop. what fits the first aphorism?
o: agree the streak is broken, so she should start over from zero tomorrow.
tell her the missed prayer cancels out the month, so she'd better double up.
the crash shows she was leaning on her streak; keep praying, and lean on mercy.
games.why: losing all hope at one slip is the sign Ibn Ata'illah names. the fix isn't to stop doing good; it's to stop resting on the record.

practice: Sit back and let the chair take your whole weight: shoulders, arms, legs, nothing held up by effort. Rest your hands palms up. For the sit, notice what it's like to be fully held without earning it.

wordCard.voice: Don't rely on deeds. The Hikam's first saying: losing all hope at a slip shows what you were leaning on. Keep doing good; lean on God.

orig.note: Arabic: al-i'timad 'ala al-'amal, relying on deeds, the opening words of the Hikam.

carryVoice: Rely on him: keep working hard, and let mercy hold the weight you were carrying alone. Two weeks, closed.

sources.ref: Ibn Ata'illah al-Iskandari, al-Hikam, aphorism 1 (losing hope at a slip is a sign of relying on deeds)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6463 (no one enters Paradise by deeds alone; 'not even me, unless God covers me with His mercy')
